_comment: The engine version each floating `latest` CI leg is EXPECTED to resolve to.
WHY THIS FILE EXISTS. A floating `latest` leg keeps us current, but it does so by ROTATING coverage
rather than accumulating it: when `latest` advances 17 -> 18, the leg that tested 17 now tests 18 and
nothing tests 17 any more. That is not hypothetical -- PostgreSQL's `latest` walked 15 -> 16 -> 17 -> 18
with nothing pinned behind it, and 15, 16 and 17 sat untested in the middle of a range we document as
The ratchet job compares each floating leg's ACTUAL server version against the value here. When an
engine releases, the job fails, and clearing it is a deliberate two-part decision:
1. pin the OUTGOING version as a new permanent leg in continuous-integration.yml (and in
scripts/run-floor-sweep.sh, and in release.yml's REQUIRED_CHECKS), or knowingly accept the hole;
2. update the value here to the new version.
Doing only (2) is how the gap comes back. The failure message says so.
Match is on the MAJOR version only -- a patch release should not redden CI.
SQL Server is resolved by MANIFEST DIGEST rather than by version string: booting it just to ask its
version means a ~1.5 GB image, an SA password and a startup wait, while MCR publishes a <year>-latest
tag per major. `latest` matching `<value>-latest` means the ceiling has not moved. An earlier draft
excluded SQL Server from this file entirely, reasoning that all its legs were pinned so there was
nothing to ratchet -- which is circular, and left the one engine that started this investigation free
to decay again the day the next version ships.
